dedupe_keys.name: economic impact on the uk of a disruption to gnss london economics 2017 and 2021 update

description: This risk and economic appraisal estimates what the United Kingdom would lose if global navigation satellite system signals became unavailable. The first study, published by London Economics in June 2017 and commissioned by Innovate UK with the UK Space Agency and the Royal Institute of Navigation, estimated that a five-day disruption would cost about £5.2 billion, made up of £1.7 billion of lost gross value added and £3.5 billion of lost utility. A 2021 update, finalised as Issue 4 in August 2023 and published by the government, re-estimated the benefits of GNSS in seven priority sectors (agriculture, aviation, emergency services, finance, maritime, rail and road) and put the cost of a seven-day national loss at £7.64 billion and of a 24-hour loss at £1.42 billion, with two more localised scenarios around critical transport infrastructure. Coverage: the United Kingdom, with sector-level estimates for scenarios of 24 hours to seven days. Format and access: free PDF reports on the London Economics website and GOV.UK. Caveats: estimates rest on assumptions about backup availability and behaviour, and on consultations, not observed outages; they exclude some sectors such as telecommunications timing. Simulation uses: cost inputs for hazard scenarios of jamming, space weather or system failure, cascading-failure analysis across sectors, and investment cases for backup systems such as eLoran. Related records: the RTI and NIST study of GPS benefits is the US equivalent, the Blackett review mapped UK dependencies, and the UK PNT policy framework of 2023 acted on them.
